name: Least-privilege RBAC and token hardening
objective: CKS › Cluster + System Hardening (15% + 15%). Drill EVERY hardening corner harder than the exam on a real multi-node kind cluster: control-plane manifest perms, kubelet read-only port + anonymous-auth + authz mode, two apiserver admission/flag hardenings, least-privilege RBAC, ServiceAccount token hardening, and a no-hint diagnose-and-fix. Graded exactly, per requirement.

questions.title: Least-privilege RBAC for a workload
questions.teach:
Give a workload the minimum API access: a narrow namespaced **Role** (only the verbs/resources needed) bound to its ServiceAccount via a **RoleBinding** — never `cluster-admin`. Imperatively: `kubectl create role r --verb=get,list --resource=pods` then `kubectl create rolebinding rb --role=r --serviceaccount=<ns>:<name>`.

**Gotcha:** `--serviceaccount` takes `ns:name`, not just the name.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `cks-learn` a ServiceAccount `reader` already exists. Create a Role granting only `get,list` on `pods` and a RoleBinding binding it to that SA.

Target: SA `reader` can `list pods` (`yes`) but cannot `delete pods` (`no`) in `cks-learn`.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n cks-learn create role pod-reader --verb=get,list --resource=pods`, then `kubectl -n cks-learn create rolebinding reader-pr --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=cks-learn:reader`.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n cks-learn create role pod-reader --verb=get,list --resource=pods
kubectl -n cks-learn create rolebinding reader-pr --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=cks-learn:reader
kubectl auth can-i list pods   --as=system:serviceaccount:cks-learn:reader -n cks-learn   # yes
kubectl auth can-i delete pods --as=system:serviceaccount:cks-learn:reader -n cks-learn   # no

verification.description: SA reader can list pods but cannot delete pods in cks-learn

questions.eli5:
Think of RBAC like giving someone a **keycard** to a building. The lazy, dangerous move is to hand out a **master keycard** (`cluster-admin`) that opens every door — if that card is stolen, the whole building is owned. **Least privilege** means: give a card that opens *only* the one door this person actually needs, and nothing else.

In Kubernetes there are two pieces:

- A **Role** is the list of what a keycard can do — e.g. "may `get` and `list` **pods**." It's scoped to one namespace (one floor of the building).
- A **RoleBinding** staples that Role to a specific **ServiceAccount** (the identity the workload runs as) — "give *this* card to *that* person."

So here you make a Role that allows only `get,list` on `pods`, then a RoleBinding that hands it to the `reader` ServiceAccount. The result: `reader` can *list* pods (allowed) but can't *delete* them (never granted). The fastest way is imperative:

```bash
kubectl -n cks-learn create role pod-reader --verb=get,list --resource=pods
kubectl -n cks-learn create rolebinding reader-pr --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=cks-learn:reader
```

**Watch out for:**

- **`--serviceaccount` wants `namespace:name`**, not just the name. `cks-learn:reader`, not `reader`. This is the classic trip-up.
- **Grant only what's needed.** Don't add `delete`, `*`, or extra resources "just in case" — that defeats least privilege and can fail the check.
- **Role + RoleBinding are a pair.** A Role alone grants nothing until something is bound to it.
- **Namespace matters.** A Role and its binding are per-namespace; create both in `cks-learn`.
- **Verify with `kubectl auth can-i ... --as=system:serviceaccount:cks-learn:reader`** — expect `yes` for list, `no` for delete.
questions.deepDive:
## Least-privilege RBAC for a workload — full rundown

### Mental model
Kubernetes RBAC is four object types in two pairs:
- **Role / ClusterRole** — *what* actions are allowed (verbs × resources × apiGroups).
- **RoleBinding / ClusterRoleBinding** — *who* gets a (Cluster)Role.

Least privilege = a **narrow namespaced Role** (only the verbs/resources the workload needs) bound to its **ServiceAccount** via a **RoleBinding**. Never grant `cluster-admin` or wildcard (`*`) to a workload.

### Role vs ClusterRole, RoleBinding vs ClusterRoleBinding
| Object | Scope | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **Role** | one namespace | namespaced permissions |
| **ClusterRole** | cluster-wide / cluster resources (nodes, PVs) | cluster or reusable perms |
| **RoleBinding** | grants Role **or** ClusterRole **within one namespace** | most least-privilege grants |
| **ClusterRoleBinding** | grants a ClusterRole **cluster-wide** | admin/system only — avoid for apps |

> A RoleBinding can reference a **ClusterRole** to reuse a definition but limit it to one namespace — a common pattern.

### Imperative creation (fastest in the exam)
```bash
kubectl -n cks-learn create role pod-reader \
  --verb=get,list --resource=pods

kubectl -n cks-learn create rolebinding reader-pr \
  --role=pod-reader \
  --serviceaccount=cks-learn:reader
```

### Equivalent YAML
```yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: pod-reader
  namespace: cks-learn
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]          # "" = core group (pods, services, configmaps...)
  resources: ["pods"]
  verbs: ["get","list"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: reader-pr
  namespace: cks-learn
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: Role
  name: pod-reader
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: reader
  namespace: cks-learn
```

### Verbs and apiGroups
| Verbs | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `get` | read one object by name |
| `list` | enumerate objects (needed for `kubectl get pods`) |
| `watch` | stream changes |
| `create`/`update`/`patch`/`delete` | writes — omit for read-only |

- Core resources (pods, services, configmaps, secrets) → `apiGroups: [""]`.
- `deployments` → `apps`; `roles` → `rbac.authorization.k8s.io`; etc. Imperative `--resource=pods` fills the group automatically.

### Verify with can-i
```bash
kubectl auth can-i list pods   --as=system:serviceaccount:cks-learn:reader -n cks-learn   # yes
kubectl auth can-i delete pods --as=system:serviceaccount:cks-learn:reader -n cks-learn   # no
```
The SA identity string is **`system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name>`**.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`--serviceaccount=ns:name`**, not just `name`. Omitting the namespace is the #1 mistake.
- **Role needs a binding.** A Role alone authorizes nothing.
- **Grant exactly what's asked.** Adding `delete`/`*`/extra resources breaks least privilege and can fail a graded check that expects `delete = no`.
- **Namespace both objects.** Role + RoleBinding live in `cks-learn`.
- **`list` ≠ `get`.** `kubectl get pods` needs `list`; a Role with only `get` can't list.
- **RoleBinding is immutable in `roleRef`** — to point at a different Role you must delete and recreate the binding.
- Use `--as=system:serviceaccount:...` to test; `can-i` evaluates real RBAC.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n cks-learn create role pod-reader --verb=get,list --resource=pods
kubectl -n cks-learn create rolebinding reader-pr --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=cks-learn:reader
kubectl auth can-i list   pods --as=system:serviceaccount:cks-learn:reader -n cks-learn   # yes
kubectl auth can-i delete pods --as=system:serviceaccount:cks-learn:reader -n cks-learn   # no
```

questions.title: ServiceAccount token hardening
questions.teach:
By default every pod auto-mounts a ServiceAccount token an attacker could steal. For pods that never call the API, set `automountServiceAccountToken: false` on the **ServiceAccount**, then point the pod at it with `serviceAccountName` so it gets no token volume.

**Gotcha:** `automountServiceAccountToken` sits at the **top level** of the SA object, not inside a `spec:` block — a common YAML mistake.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `cks-learn`, create a ServiceAccount `no-token` with `automountServiceAccountToken: false`, then run a pod `hardened` (image `busybox:1.36`, e.g. `sleep 3600`) using that ServiceAccount.

Target: SA `no-token` has `automountServiceAccountToken: false` AND pod `hardened` runs as SA `no-token` with no SA token volume mounted.
questions.hint: Create the SA with `automountServiceAccountToken: false` (top level), then create the pod with `serviceAccountName: no-token`. Apply with `kubectl apply -f -`.
questions.solution:
kubectl apply -f - <<'YAML'
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: no-token
  namespace: cks-learn
automountServiceAccountToken: false
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: hardened
  namespace: cks-learn
spec:
  serviceAccountName: no-token
  containers:
  - name: c
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
YAML

verification.description: SA no-token has automount disabled and pod hardened uses it with no token mounted

questions.eli5:
Every pod, by default, gets handed a little **access token** on the way in — a pass that lets code inside the pod talk to the cluster's apiserver. That's convenient *if* the pod needs to call the API. But most pods don't! And a token sitting unused inside a pod is a free gift to an attacker: break into the container, grab the token, and now they can knock on the apiserver's door as that identity. It's like giving every delivery driver a key to the server room "just in case" — most never need it, and each spare key is a risk.

The hardening move: for pods that never call the API, **don't hand out the token at all**. You do that by setting `automountServiceAccountToken: false` on the **ServiceAccount**, then pointing your pod at that ServiceAccount with `serviceAccountName`. Result: the pod mounts no token volume — no key to steal.

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata: { name: no-token, namespace: cks-learn }
automountServiceAccountToken: false      # top level!
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: hardened, namespace: cks-learn }
spec:
  serviceAccountName: no-token
  containers:
  - { name: c, image: busybox:1.36, command: ["sleep","3600"] }
```

**Watch out for:**

- **`automountServiceAccountToken` is a TOP-LEVEL field on the ServiceAccount**, NOT inside a `spec:` block. ServiceAccounts have no `spec`. This is the classic YAML mistake.
- **The pod must actually use the SA** — set `serviceAccountName: no-token`. Otherwise it uses `default` and still gets a token.
- **You can also set it per-pod** (`spec.automountServiceAccountToken: false` on the Pod) — and the pod-level setting *overrides* the SA-level one if both are present.
- **Same namespace.** The SA and the pod both live in `cks-learn`.
questions.deepDive:
## ServiceAccount token hardening — full rundown

### Mental model
Every namespace has a `default` ServiceAccount, and by default every pod **auto-mounts that SA's token** at `/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token`. Code in the pod can present that token to the apiserver as the SA identity. For pods that never call the API, the token is pure attack surface — a stolen token = API access as that SA. Hardening = **suppress the token mount** for pods that don't need it, via `automountServiceAccountToken: false`.

### Where the setting lives
| Object | Field path | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **ServiceAccount** | `automountServiceAccountToken` (**top level**) | SAs have **no `spec`** — the field is a sibling of `metadata` |
| **Pod** | `spec.automountServiceAccountToken` | pod-level, inside `spec` |

**Precedence:** if both are set, the **pod-level** value wins over the SA-level value.

### The manifest
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: no-token
  namespace: cks-learn
automountServiceAccountToken: false     # TOP LEVEL, not under spec
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: hardened
  namespace: cks-learn
spec:
  serviceAccountName: no-token          # pod must use the hardened SA
  containers:
  - name: c
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
```

### Two ways to achieve "no token"
| Approach | Set on | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| SA-level | `automountServiceAccountToken: false` on the SA | every pod using that SA gets no token (unless the pod overrides) |
| Pod-level | `spec.automountServiceAccountToken: false` on the Pod | just that pod, regardless of SA |

The lab wants the **SA-level** flag plus a pod that uses the SA.

### Verify
```bash
# SA has the flag
kubectl -n cks-learn get sa no-token -o jsonpath='{.automountServiceAccountToken}'; echo   # false

# pod uses the SA and has NO token volume/mount
kubectl -n cks-learn get pod hardened -o jsonpath='{.spec.serviceAccountName}'; echo        # no-token
kubectl -n cks-learn get pod hardened -o yaml | grep -i serviceaccount
# there should be no kube-api-access-* projected volume / mount

# prove it from inside:
kubectl -n cks-learn exec hardened -- ls /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount 2>&1
# -> No such file or directory
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`automountServiceAccountToken` is top-level on the SA** — a ServiceAccount has no `spec:`. Nesting it under `spec:` silently does nothing (and may be rejected).
- **The pod must reference the SA** via `serviceAccountName: no-token`. Omit it and the pod falls back to `default` and still mounts a token.
- **Pod-level overrides SA-level.** If a pod sets `spec.automountServiceAccountToken: true`, it gets a token even with a hardened SA.
- **Same namespace** for SA and pod (`cks-learn`).
- **This removes the auto-mount, not RBAC.** Even a mounted token only grants whatever RBAC the SA has — but removing it closes the theft vector entirely.
- Modern tokens are short-lived, bound, projected volumes (`kube-api-access-*`); hardening removes that projected volume.

### Quick reference
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata: { name: no-token, namespace: cks-learn }
automountServiceAccountToken: false      # top level
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: hardened, namespace: cks-learn }
spec:
  serviceAccountName: no-token
  containers:
  - { name: c, image: busybox:1.36, command: ["sleep","3600"] }
```
```bash
kubectl -n cks-learn exec hardened -- ls /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount   # no such dir
```
